conflicts.point: Whether large-scale pre-training clusters exceeding 10 to the 26th power floating-point operations can be effectively monitored without driving open-source developers out of the market.

positions.stance: Large-scale frontier pre-training clusters are physically massive and centralized enough to be regulated at the corporate boundary without capturing everyday hardware or harming open-source developers.
Frontier capabilities can be trained on smaller, distributed commodity clusters or via algorithmic efficiency gains, rendering training-cluster thresholds porous and obsolete.

verdicts.conflict: Whether large-scale pre-training clusters exceeding 10 to the 26th power floating-point operations can be effectively monitored without driving open-source developers out of the market.
verdicts.rationale: Both sides present valid empirical points that currently lack definitive reconciliation. Safety advocates correctly identify that current frontier models require massive capital investments and physical data centers. Skeptics and accelerationists correctly note that algorithmic gains reduce compute requirements over time, while compliance costs genuinely harm small developers. The dispute remains balanced because neither side has proven whether future algorithmic efficiency will outpace hardware monitoring capabilities.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal data on whether hardware telemetry compliance forces independent AI labs out of business while successfully intercepting malicious frontier training runs.
